chunks.content: Editors-in-Chief Statement Regarding Published Clinical Trials Conducted without IRB Approval by Joachim Boldt March 12, 2011 To our readers: Landesärztekammer Rheinland-Pfalz (“LÄK-RLP”), the State Medical Association of Rheinland-Pfalz, Germany serves as the Institutional Review Board (IRB) for clinical research at Klinikum Ludwigshafen, where Dr. Joachim Boldt’s recent research was conducted. On February 25, 2011, LÄK-RLP provided the involved journals with the results of their evaluation of the status of IRB approval for research conducted by Dr. Boldt dating back to 1999. LÄK- RLP determined, to the best of its ability, the status of IRB approval for 102 articles published by Dr. Boldt. Table 1 lists 88 articles for which LÄK-RLP was unable to verify IRB approval. Table 2 lists 12 articles for which LÄK-RLP was able to verify IRB approval. Table 3 lists 2 articles for which LÄK-RLP determined that IRB approval was not necessary. The undersigned Editors-in-Chief of medical journals affected by these findings will retract the articles in our respective journals that are listed in table 1. Formal retraction notices will appear in each journal. The retraction of the articles in Table 1 for lack of IRB approval means that the research was unethical, and that IRB approval for the research was misrepresented in the published article. It does not mean that the research results per se are fraudulent. Klinikum Ludwigshafen has commissioned an investigating committee to systematically assess the veracity of the findings presented in Dr. Boldt’s articles against patient and laboratory records. We will communicate to our readers any finding of data fabrication, falsification, or misrepresentation identified by the investigating committee at Klinikum Ludwigshafen. We, the undersigned Editors-in-Chief, on behalf of our Editorial Boards, affiliated societies, and publishers, extend our appreciation to LÄK-RLP for their review of the status of IRB approval for Dr. Boldt’s research and to the investigating committee at Klinikum Ludwigshafen for their ongoing review of his research findings. Amendments: 1. March 4, 2011: LÄK-RLP has verified IRB approval for Boldt J, Schöllhorn T, Münchbach J, Pabsdorf M. A total balanced volume replacement strategy using a new balanced hydoxyethyl starch preparation (6% HES 130/0.42) in patients undergoing major abdominal surgery. Eur J Anaesthesiol. 2007;24:267-75. This article was moved from table 1 (articles without documented IRB approval) to table 2 (articles with documented IRB approval). 2. March 12, 2011: Markus K. LÄK- RLP determined, to the best of its ability, the status of IRB approval for 102 articles published by Dr. Boldt. Table 1 lists 88 articles for which LÄK-RLP was unable to verify IRB approval. The undersigned Editors-in-Chief of medical journals affected by these findings will retract the articles in our respective journals that are listed in table 1. Formal retraction notices will appear in each journal. The retraction of the articles in Table 1 for lack of IRB approval means that the research was unethical, and that IRB approval for the research was misrepresented in the published article. It does not mean that the research results per se are fraudulent. Klinikum Ludwigshafen has commissioned an investigating committee to systematically assess the veracity of the findings presented in Dr. Boldt’s articles against patient and laboratory records. We will communicate to our readers any finding of data fabrication, falsification, or misrepresentation identified by the investigating committee at Klinikum Ludwigshafen. We, the undersigned Editors-in-Chief, on behalf of our Editorial Boards, affiliated societies, and publishers, extend our appreciation to LÄK-RLP for their review of the status of IRB approval for Dr. Boldt’s research and to the investigating committee at Klinikum Ludwigshafen for their ongoing review of his research findings. Background Cardiac surgery is characterized by altered haemostasis and increased risk of bleeding [ ]. Moderate and excessive bleeding concern 40% and 10% of the patients respectively [ , ]. Both moderate/excessive bleeding and transfusion and/or prescription of blood-derived products are independently associated with an increased risk of death [ , , – ]. Because the effectiveness and the benefit-to-risk ratio of blood products are debated [ – ], blood-derived products, e.g. prothrombin complex concentrate or fibrinogen concentrate have been proposed as first-line therapies to correct haemostasis abnormalities following cardiac surgery and to decrease the use of blood products and their side effects [ , ]. Among coagulation factors, fibrinogen concentration is the first to decrease below a critical threshold during cardiac surgery and thus contributes to increase the risk of bleeding [ ]. Several studies have suggested that low pre-operative and/or low post-operative fibrinogen concentration is strongly associated with an increased risk of bleeding [ ]. These observational studies have been the incentive to perform interventional studies to test the hypothesis that correction of acquired hypofibrinogenemia with fibrinogen concentrate could decrease bleeding and transfusion of blood products following cardiac surgery [ – ]. These studies and meta-analyses [ , ] have been the basis of recommendations by scientific societies for using fibrinogen concentrate in cardiac surgery [ – ]. In 2013, then in subsequent 2017/2022 updates, the European Society of Anaesthesiology (ESA; ESAIC since 2020) recommended treatment with fibrinogen concentrate in bleeding patients [ – ]. Other narrative/systematic reviews have also adopted similar recommendations [ , ]. Guidelines are aimed at stating on actual scientific knowledge and to incentive practitioners to homogenize their clinical practice, and, in this case of cardiac surgery, at reducing the high variability on blood and blood-derived products prescriptions among institutions (or clinicians from the same institution) [ , ]. To the best of our knowledge, there are no prospective studies that investigated compliance with the ESAIC guidelines concerning the prescription of fibrinogen concentrate in adult patients undergoing cardiac surgery. Evaluating compliance is important to assess their practical performance in clinical settings, which may result from two main features, comprehensibility and applicability. Furthermore, analysis of compliance with published guidelines could have an impact on subsequent guidelines updates/implementation tools [ , ]. This study evaluates compliance with ESAIC guidelines on fibrinogen concentrate prescription in cardiac surgery and explores its impact on outcomes. Patients and methods Patient population Adult patients (older than 18 years), who underwent cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) consecutively between March 09, 2017, and April 10, 2018, were recruited. As no ethical issues were raised by establishing a non-interventional registry, the study was not submitted to relevant Independent Ethics Committees/Institutional Review Boards. All included patients gave informed consent for the use of their medical records related to the study. Study design and setting The FibCard study was a multicentre, cohort, observational study conducted in 13 French cardiac surgery centres (list of centres at the end of the manuscript). According to the ESAIC guidelines, a fibrinogen concentration of less than 1.5 to 2 g.l-1 was considered as acquired hypofibrinogenemia. However, the treatment of hypofibrinogenemia with fibrinogen concentrate was recommended only in bleeding patients [ , ]. For the current study, hypofibrinogenemia was defined whenever plasma fibrinogen was < 2 g.l-1. Since there is no consensus on the definition of bleeding in real-time, the study steering committee agreed to consider only postoperative blood loss in the drains to define bleeding patients. When the total volume of blood collected from chest tubes at H-24 of chest closure exceeded the 75th percentile of the cohort, patients were considered as having “clinically relevant postoperative bleeding”. Therefore, adherence to guidelines meant either: 1) fibrinogen concentrate prescription for patients with plasma fibrinogen < 2 g.l-1 AND having postoperative clinically relevant bleeding, or 2) no fibrinogen concentrate prescription for patients with fibrinogen ≥ 2 g.l-1 AND/OR without postoperative clinically relevant bleeding. Fibrinogen plasma concentration was collected during surgery and within the first 48 postoperative hours according to the routine clinical practice of each centre. The chronology and conditions of FC prescriptions (i.e. time of prescription, the delay between the first and the second prescription, and doses) were also recorded. The compliance to ESAIC guidelines was then checked, allowing to classify patients into 4 groups according to adherence to recommendations (R) (R ±) and fibrinogen concentrate (FC) administration (FC ±): Group 1: FC recommended, and FC administered (R +/FC +). Group 2: FC recommended, and FC not administered (R +/FC-). Group 3: FC not recommended, and FC administered (R-/FC +). Group 4: FC not recommended, and FC not administered (R-/FC-). The allocation of the patients to one of the four groups was performed with automated coding using Excel software and checked by an adjudication committee on anonymized centre data. Data verification was performed remotely by trained clinical research assistants to ensure data quality. Study size Sample size estimation was based on an anticipated 10% prevalence of patients with severe bleeding after cardiac surgery who would require the prescription of FC.2,3 In a population of 3000 patients, 300 patients may receive fibrinogen concentrate with a good compliance to guidelines. We anticipated that further 150 to 250 patients may be exposed to fibrinogen concentrate prescription, though not in the massive bleeding group, possibly outside the guidelines. Therefore, up to 500 ± 50 patients can be exposed to FC prescription. No power analysis was conducted for secondary outcomes. Statistical analyses Continuous data are expressed as mean ± standard deviation or for non-normal distribution, median [25;75 percentiles]. Categorical variables are expressed as the number and percentage of documented categories (n, %). No replacement of missing data was performed. The primary endpoint was estimated with its 2-sided 95% confidence interval (95%CI). A negative binomial mixed model using a pseudo-likelihood method of estimation was used to estimate the association of compliance with the Guidelines and FC prescription with death, after adjustment (fixed factors) on the type of surgery, CPB time, and prescription of blood products (as Incidence Risk Ratio, IRR). Hospital length of stay was considered as a surrogate of postoperative complications. A generalized mixed model (multinomial) was used to estimate the association of FC prescription with hospital duration (terciles, using a generalized mixed model, with ordinal distribution and cumulative logit) in non-deceased patients, after adjustment (fixed factors) on type of surgery, CPB time and prescription of blood products. All estimates are IRR. The study centre was entered as a random effect in mixed models. All statistical tests were 2-sided and at the 0.05 significant threshold. However, level 2 interactions were tested at the 0.10 statistically significant level. Statistically significant interactions were graphically explored. Statistical analysis was performed using SAS® Version 9.4, and SAS/STAT 15.1 software (SAS Institute, North Carolina USA). First, documented hypofibrinogenemia implies measurement and there might be analytical variability when measuring fibrinogen concentration [ ]. Besides, we observed a contextual interpretation of acquired hypofibrinogenemia, since the prescription of FC was mostly motivated by other reason than plasma fibrinogen concentration itself (> 60%). Second, the recommendation infers a"clinically relevant bleeding". This term is even more"uncertain"mostly because clinicians need to identify clinically relevant bleeding in real-time, especially in the operating room with the thorax open. Except for clinically obvious situations, practitioners often make"bets"(probabilistic reasoning) on excessive bleeding, possibly based on predictive scores [ ]. However, their predictive positive values are low, even when adding viscoelastic tests [ , ]. Incorporating real time bleeding may be more approachable in postoperative care. In a prospective observational study, early bleeding within the first 2 postoperative hours in the ICU was shown to predict high blood loss at 12 h. Thus, blood products or FC administration could be objectively prescribed early, before further bleeding occurs [ ]. Furthermore, clinically relevant bleeding is not only a matter of definition but also of the physician's estimate of"clinical relevance", which may vary according to centres, physicians, surgical procedures, or patients [ ]. Our definition of excessive bleeding aimed at overcoming these difficulties. However, the 75th percentile volume observed in our cohort was only 720 ml. According to the Universal Definition of Perioperative Bleeding classification, a volume of 601- 800 ml at 12 h is considered as mild bleeding [ ]. Thus, our estimation of the incidence estimate of clinically relevant postoperative bleeding may appear high as our threshold was very low. Conversely, an absence of postoperative bleeding following a timely, pertinent FC administration in the operating room (representing most prescriptions in our cohort: 56.4%), may have resulted in overestimating undue FC prescription. Compliance with the ESAIC guidelines appeared rather high (86.5%) despite a large variation in FC prescription between centres [ ]. The high level of compliance was mainly driven by the adherence to non-indication of FC (94.9%), meaning physicians did not prescribe FC when it was not recommended. The low number of FC prescription while recommended (5%) further suggests that physicians were reluctant to use fibrinogen concentrate. Consequently, non-compliance appears rather limited (13.5%), even if “over-prescription” (9.1%) exceeded “under-prescription” (4.4%). Anyway, these numbers should be interpreted with caution due to the weakness in the ESAIC guidelines in interpreting bleeding in real-time and excluding possible adequate anticipation of a bleeding risk. Though non-compliance with the ESAIC Guidelines was rather limited, the question arose of whether non-compliance, as well as FC prescription, might be associated with the risk of poor outcomes, i.e., in-hospital death or postoperative complications (integrated into intensive care unit/hospital length of stay for surviving patients). Our results did not show statistically significant association but demonstrated that factors independently associated with an increased risk of death or complications were the type of surgery, the CPB time, and the prescription of blood products. Of note, patients who received FC had more complex surgeries and lower platelet counts that could have impacted the outcomes. Although the statistical association is not causality, given the widely documented evidence on the association between blood products transfusion and patient outcome, one could be tempted to assert that unnecessary prescription of blood products is deleterious and should be avoided especially since this is a modifiable factor as opposed to the type of surgery or CPB time [ , ]. This study has some limitations. It reflects French cardiac surgery practices in academic hospitals. Although all clinicians were aware of the 2017 ESAIC guidelines and the recommendations for the prescription of FC, there was no effort to develop a common definition of excessive bleeding in real time. The criterion based on total blood loss from chest tubes within 24 h after surgery was defined posteriori. The absence of bleeding definition contemporary to hypofibrinogenemia, may have induced some bias in patients’ classification especially during the operative period. Furthermore, prescription of FC and blood products was only very rarely based on viscoelastic tests, which were used in few centres only at this time. A more frequent use of viscoelastic tests would possibly have changed the way clinicians diagnosed haemostasis abnormalities. The lack of association between compliance with the guidelines and poor outcomes should be interpreted with caution, due to the low number of events (in-hospital deaths), and no adjustment to a mortality score (Euroscore II). Furthermore, the FibCard study was conceived on the 2017 ESAIC Guidelines, and because of COVID-19, the interpretation of the results was delayed. The major strength of the study was to evaluate ESAIC guidelines implementation, and consequences on outcomes, in several cardiac surgery centres. It is acknowledged that any guidelines development should be associated with implementation strategies and follow-up on compliance/non-compliance and their impact on outcomes [ , ]. The study design underlines the difficulties in formulating recommendations explicitly enough so that they can be applied without ambiguity and to induce homogenous clinical decision-making [ , ]. These findings could also be an incentive for the experts who participate in guidelines development to give clearer guidance on real-time bleeding assessment and standardized decision-support tools to optimize FC use. In conclusion, compliance with ESAIC guidelines was high, but we observed a large inter-centre variability in FC prescription. Over-prescription was more common than under-prescription, likely due to uncertainty in bleeding assessment. Non-compliance was not associated with adverse outcomes, but our findings highlight the need for clearer clinical decision tools to facilitate the management of FC in cardiac surgical patients. chunks.content: KEY POINTS Question: How long do patients abstain from drinking clear fluids before surgery? Can this time be reduced, and does it benefit patients and hospitals to do so? Findings: Adherence to a fluid-fasting time of 2 to 4 hours was 40% and could be increased over time with evidence showing a decrease in postoperative delirium in the recovery room, hospital length of stay, and patient-reported outcomes for short (2–4 hours) in comparison with longer times. Meaning: Preoperative fluid-fasting times can and should be reduced to 2 to 4 hours in clinical practice whenever possible. See Article, page 1098 Traditionally, patients were advised to abstain from solids or liquids after midnight before elective surgeries, called “nil by mouth after midnight,” to decrease the risk of vomiting and aspiration. Applying this approach, however, frequently resulted in prolonged fluid-fasting times (FFT) of up to 12 to 20 hours. – Beginning in 1999, professional anesthesiology bodies reduced their guidance for FFT of clear liquids to 2 hours to improve patient well-being without increasing aspiration risk, – which is supported by a meta-analysis of randomized trials. Despite guidelines having changed over 3 decades ago, patients still fast for a median of up to 12 h before anesthesia, mainly due to organizational challenges. Studies have identified obstacles such as reduced surgical scheduling flexibility, communication barriers, and the risk of aspiration if FFT is less than 2 hours. – Additionally, patients’ own concerns and often a lack of a clearly communicated fasting-initiation time complicate the adoption of these practices. When modifying fluid-fasting practices, patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) are indispensable for capturing patients’ experiences throughout the perioperative period. This includes their feelings of thirst, discomfort, or anxiety related to fasting. During a quality-improvement initiative implementing the Safe Brain Initiative care bundle (SBI-CB) containing 18 perioperative guidelines for improving patient safety at 4 hospitals in Denmark and Turkey, PROMs were collected alongside FFT, total hospital stay, and postoperative delirium (POD) in the postoperative care unit (PACU). , The primary hypothesis of this work was that adherence to short FFT increased over time, and the secondary hypothesis was that patients benefited from a short FFT in comparison to a long FFT in clinical practice in terms of POD in the PACU, hospital length of stay (LOS), and PROMs. METHODS Study Design and Participants We present a multicenter, retrospective cohort analysis of data extracted from the SBI database. This dataset was described and published in previous work. The data were collected at 4 participating hospitals, 3 from Denmark and one from Turkey. The Danish Data Protection Agency granted permission for patient data collection (REG-041-2017, REG-041-2017, and REG-117-2019 for the Danish sites, respectively). As data collection was within the framework of a quality-improvement initiative, no permission was required from the Danish Scientific Ethics Committees as recorded in the case file J. No. 17-000048. The implementation of the SBI-CB was accepted as a quality development initiative and was approved by the Human Research Ethics Committee of Ankara University Faculty of Medicine under ethical approval number I2-88-21. No clinical trial was registered for this retrospective analysis of previously published work. Reporting follows Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) guidelines for cohort studies. A general summary of each participating hospital and data are given in the Supplemental Digital Content 1, Supplemental Table 1, https://links.lww.com/AA/F561 . Extracted data encompassed adult patients, ≥18 years, who were scheduled for elective and semi-elective surgery; emergency surgeries were excluded due to urgency. There were no other exclusion criteria; however, patients needed to be able to communicate with the healthcare staff to establish PROMs. Data were collected for a convenience sample of patients and were not exhaustive to all patients. The Approach to Decreasing FFT As a retrospective analysis of previously collected data, the presented work did not involve a clinical intervention. In the following, however, the steps taken by the previously published SBI-CB to decrease FFT are described. The SBI-CB included education of staff to increase adherence to evidence-based preoperative fasting guidelines, particularly focusing on reducing FFT to 2 hours before surgery. Staff could track their average FFT and assess patient thirst levels using feedback from the SBI dashboard, which increased awareness. Fluid fasting was consistently addressed as a recurring agenda item in morning meetings with cross-functional clinical teams. In addition, regular communication between hospital SBI-CB coordinators enabled the exchange of challenges and solutions. Site 3 took additional steps including (1) emailing relevant perioperative staff with information about fluid-fasting protocols; (2) structured education by providing in-person training for anesthesia and surgical teams and distributing posters and patient information brochures in premedication clinics and ambulatory clinics. Trained nurses and medical students performed data collection and digital database transfer. Data were stored according to European Union data-protection regulations with access strictly limited to authorized personnel via the clinical trial management system, EasyTrial. For this work, the relevant pseudo-anonymized dataset was extracted directly from the database by EasyTrial and securely transferred to the authors for analysis, as authorized by the data controllers. Patient and Procedure Characteristics Data were available for sex, age, American Society of Anesthesia (ASA) Physical Status Classification System (referred to as ASA I–V), surgical duration in hours, and type of anesthesia. For anesthesia type, we divided the patients into 2 categories based on the highest level of anesthesia administered: “General” (encompassing any patient receiving general anesthesia) or “Other” (encompassing any combination of procedural sedation and local anesthesia without general anesthesia). Surgical categories were not classified uniformly across sites. Supplemental Digital Content 1, Supplementary Table 1, https://links.lww.com/AA/F561 provides the surgical categories as recorded per site and the respective patient counts, along with sex, age, and ASA classifications. Other patient or procedure characteristics were either not available or too sparse for data analysis. Primary Outcome The primary outcome was adherence to FFT guidelines overall and over time (per month since the SBI care bundle started). FFT was reported in hours by the patient, where the patient provided estimates in whole hours of their last consumption of more than 200 mL of clear liquid before anesthetic induction. For the analysis, FFT was categorized into short FFT (2–4 hours) and long FFT (5–24 hours). The few patients with FFT less than 2 hours and greater than 24 hours were excluded as outliers (Supplemental Digital Content 2, Supplemental Figure 1, https://links.lww.com/AA/F562 ). We considered adherence to guidelines was achieved when a patient fasted between 2 and 4 hours, a time-frame that was used for evidence reporting in the most recent ASA guidelines for fluid fasting, because we required a broader time-frame for analyzing FFT rather than precisely 2 hours, which is mentioned in all guidelines. – Secondary Outcomes The secondary outcomes in this study include several clinical and patient-reported measures. These secondary outcomes were assessed by comparing short and long FFT patient cohorts, depending on available data for each comparison: 1. Data from all 4 hospital sites were combined, resulting in an original dataset of 18,697 patients: 12,783 from Site 1, 2121 from Site 2, 1458 from Site 3, and 2335 from Site 4. Due to the SBI-CB mass data collection, some data points were missing from most variables, leading to smaller cohorts being analyzed. Patients with missing data were excluded on a per-analysis basis to maximize the number of patients available. Patient numbers were consistently reported per analysis. Patients with an FFT of less than 2 hours (N = 49), FFT greater than 24 hours (N = 19), and patients with a hospital LOS of zero hours (N = 195) were excluded from the analysis. In addition, we excluded patients with ≥ 363 hours (2 weeks) of hospital LOS as we assumed long-term hospital stays were likely due to serious illness, which was not a focus. A maximum of 15,837 patients were included after filtering (see Supplemental Digital Content 2, Supplemental Figure 1, https://links.lww.com/AA/F562 for filtering details). Adherence to short FFT was calculated as the proportion of patients in the short FFT group out of all patients that were treated in the month after the SBI was implemented at each site. Adherence to short FFT was analyzed in the combined data and by hospital site separately. To analyze the effect of FFT on patient outcomes, we separated patients into short FFT (2–4 hours) and long FFT (5–24 hours) groups. The correlation of the proportion of patients in the short FFT group (ie, the percentage of patients adherent to guidelines) with the month since the SBI-CB was initiated per hospital was calculated using Pearson’s method. Correlation analyses were performed on combined data, and per hospital, the correlation coefficient, r, was reported alongside the p-value. To account for confounding effects between short and long FFT cohorts, we performed an optimal full (one-to-many) patient matching (MatchIT package v4.5.4 in R). The distance was estimated with logistic regression. Balance of confounders was tested by a standardized difference ≤ 0.1. The confounders included were sex, age (categorized into 18–35 years, 36–55 years, 56–75 years, and >75 years), ASA score (categorized as I/II, III+), surgery time (categorized into ≤ 1 hour, 1–2 hours, and >2 hours), and anesthesia type (general, other). The impact of short vs long FFT on patient outcomes was assessed in the matched patient dataset. Since all the continuous variables were not normally distributed, central tendency and data dispersion were reported as median and interquartile range (Q1–Q3), respectively. The statistical difference of population cohorts was assessed using the non-parametric Wilcoxon Rank Sum test for the PROMs (applied to the original NRS scale) and hospital LOS. The difference in POD in the PACU and preoperative delirium was assessed using the χ² test as binary variables. NRS scores for PROMs were binned into groups for visualization purposes only (0–3, 4–6, 7–10) as the mean and median were not good summary statistics for these outcomes. We applied the Bonferroni correction to account for multiple comparisons, adjusting the significance threshold for 13 comparisons, resulting in a revised alpha level of p = 0.0038. The remaining 59.7% (N = 9456) fell into the longer FFT category (Figure A). Prolonged FFT of at least 12 hours was experienced by 11.9% (N = 1888) of patients. We observed a significant positive correlation between SBI-CB months of implementation and the adherence rate to short FFT times (Pearson’s correlation coefficient r = 0.7, p-value<0.001, Figure B). When stratified by hospital site, all sites showed a positive correlation trend; however, only Site 3 achieved a significant increase in adherence to short FFT times (r = 0.5, P = .02, see Supplemental Digital Content 3, Supplemental Figure 2, https://links.lww.com/AA/F563 ) likely due to the additional measures taken by Site 3 to reduce FFT. It is important to note that there is heterogeneity between the sites in terms of number of patients, sex, age, ASA category, and the distribution of general procedure categories—and likely in other measurements also (Supplemental Digital Content 1, Supplemental Table 1, https://links.lww.com/AA/F561 ). Comparison Between Short and Long FFT The secondary outcomes look at the impact of short versus long FFT on PROMs, POD reported in the PACU, and use of hospital resources as estimated by hospital LOS. Not all relevant patient and procedure characteristics were available for assessing their confounding influence on reported outcomes. Patient and Procedure Characteristics for Short and Long FFT Patient characteristics are presented in Table . All characteristics were significantly different between short and long patient cohorts ( P < .05). In the short FFT group, the following differences in comparison to long FFT existed: more females, older median age, shorter surgical time, fewer patients with a low ASA category, and more patients having general surgery. Given these results, it is possible that the typical patient adhering to short FFT may be different from those with long FFT, although differences were statistically significant but not substantial (Table ). In addition, adjustments for confounding factors were clearly required when analyzing the impact of short versus long FFT on patient outcomes (Supplemental Digital Content 4, Supplemental Figure 3, https://links.lww.com/AA/F564 ). Measured Differences in PROMs In the matched cohort, significant differences in postoperative outcomes were found, favoring the short FFT group (Table ), including reductions in pain, stress, anxiety, nausea, and vomiting, while general well-being with a high score (NRS=7–10) increased roughly 5 percentage points from 84.7% to 89.5% ( P < .001). Preoperative well-being remained unaffected across both groups. Thirst was significantly decreased in the short FFT cohort preoperatively—not postoperatively. Fluid Fasting and POD After patient matching, the incidence of POD was slightly lower in the short FFT cohort compared to the long FFT cohort (4.3% vs 6.0%, P < .001), with no significant difference in preoperative delirium. As a complementary analysis, we performed a multivariate logistic regression including all measured patient and procedure characteristics as variables to control for their confounding influence on POD (Figure A and Supplemental Digital Content 5, Supplemental Table 2, https://links.lww.com/AA/F565 ). The logistic regression showed a significant reduction in the likelihood of developing POD for patients with short FFT (odds ratio = 0.8, 95% confidence interval (CI), [0.7–1.0], P = .03, Supplemental Digital Content 5, Supplemental Table 2, https://links.lww.com/AA/F565 ). The logistic regression also controlled for site as a further confounding factor for developing POD. A significant difference was observed for Site 2 in comparison to Site 1 but not for Sites 3 and 4. This can be easily explained because Site 2 reported comparatively few events of POD and was a surgical department for breast surgery for females only whereas the other sites included a broad range of surgeries and both sexes (Supplemental Digital Content 1, Supplemental Table 1, https://links.lww.com/AA/F561 ). When stratifying by POD, patients in the short FFT group had shorter median hospital stays by approximately 18 and 20 hours for patients without and with POD. Although the difference was more pronounced for patients with POD, results indicate that the decrease in hospital LOS is caused by further factors in addition to POD. The existence of factors beyond POD for the decrease in hospital LOS is supported by the widespread improvement in postoperative PROMs for the short FFT cohort reported in Table . A decrease in hospital LOS for patients with a short FFT is further confirmed when examining FFT as a predictor of hospital LOS in a multivariate linear regression while adjusting for available confounders (Figure B): short FFT was identified as an independent factor in reducing hospital LOS with an effect size reduction of −1.8 (95% CI, −3.1 to −0.5], P < .007). In comparison, development of POD in the PACU was associated with the greatest increase in hospital LOS (effect size 14.7 [11.3–17.5], P < .0001), followed by increased stay for patients with delirium at induction, longer surgical times, higher ASA category, and higher age, (Figure B and Supplemental Digital Content 6, Supplementary Table 3, https://links.lww.com/AA/F566 ). Hospital LOS was decreased with the greatest effect for patients receiving general anesthesia (effect size −13.0 [–14.5 to 11.6], P < .0001) (Figure B and Supplemental Digital Content 6, Supplemental Table 3, https://links.lww.com/AA/F566 ). When analyzing site as a confounding factor in the linear regression for hospital LOS, we observed that Site 2 had shorter stays and Site 4 had longer stays in general. DISCUSSION This multicenter, observational investigation, involving a large cohort of 15,837 patients, demonstrates the importance of FFT in preoperative care. Results show that shorter FFTs (2–4 hours) were associated with better postoperative outcomes, including reduced POD in the PACU, hospital stays, and overall patient well-being. Our findings have substantial clinical implications, suggesting that shorter preoperative fasting can improve patient outcomes. There is limited prior research on the impact of preoperative FFT times on the development of POD. Radtke et al identified preoperative fasting as an independent risk factor for POD in the PACU. Our study aligns with these findings, showing a decrease in POD incidence in the PACU from 6% to 4% when FFT is reduced to 2 to 4 hours, after patient matching. In a complementary multivariate logistic regression, short FFT was a significant protective factor in the development of POD in the PACU, while correcting for confounding patient and procedure characteristics including age, sex, surgery time, use of general anestheisa, ASA classification as an estimation of general co-morbidities, delirium at induction to capture those patients with symptoms of delirium before surgery, and hospital site as a proxy for structural differences between the hospitals. The reduction in POD in the PACU in the short FFT group may be influenced by multiple factors, including the combined effect of worse PROM scores, such as pain, which is a known risk factor for POD. Our results align with expected pathophysiological outcomes: allowing patients to drink preoperatively reduces their anxiety, stress, thirst, nausea, and vomiting both before and after surgery. , – While our findings on preoperative thirst reduction with shorter FFT are consistent with most research, there are varying intraoperative fluid and electrolyte management approaches across studies, making results difficult to compare. , , – We also present a reduction in total hospital LOS of 18 and 20 hours for patients adhering to short FFT—without and with POD in the PACU, respectively. Data suggest that other factors, in addition to POD, contribute to the decrease in LOS. Introducing the SBI-CB involved training and education for healthcare providers and patients about the 2-hour FFT recommendation. Despite these efforts, a significant portion of patients (60%) did not adhere to the optimal fasting time, underscoring the need for further refinement of the protocols. However, in Site 3, a more pronounced and significant reduction of overall FFT could be achieved, indicating that more structured multi-layered interventions can effectively improve the implementation and adherence to optimal fasting times. This suggests that combining various strategies, such as staff education, patient education, regular monitoring, and feedback mechanisms, may lead to substantial improvements in fluid-fasting practices, ultimately benefiting patient outcomes and overall healthcare efficiency. The strength of this study is the large and diverse cohort of 15,837 patients, offering a comprehensive and representative analysis of the impact of FFT times on postoperative outcomes across different types of surgeries. Its multicenter approach, encompassing data from several hospitals, enhances the generalizability of the findings across various clinical settings. Including PROMs adds a valuable dimension to the study, providing insights into the subjective experiences of patients undergoing surgery. Furthermore, we assessed the robustness of the POD in the PACU and hospital LOS outcomes by using complementary statistical analysis that together with previous research underscore the potential benefit of shortening FFT to 2 to 4 hours for patients and hospitals. This study has several limitations. The retrospective cohort design introduces inherent limitations of potential biases in data collection and an inability to establish direct causality. While the study used statistical methods to control for known confounding factors, there remains the possibility that unmeasured variables could have affected the results such as various specific co-morbidities, further risk factors for delirium, surgery start time, intraoperative events, type of surgery, and further site-specific heterogeneity. The differences between the sites can be seen as both a strength and a limitation for introducing bias. The intention of this work was to include as many patients for analysis as possible, whereas missing values and an unbalanced numbers of patients from the sites are a limitation of this analysis. Matching based on site did not lead to a sufficient number of patients for analysis in all outcomes but site was included in the regression analyses as a confounding factor. Moreover, as a long-term, quality-improvement initiative that evolved over time, there was no control or baseline for statistical analysis, further complicating the interpretation of results. Having missing datapoints in most variables raises the concern about the accuracy and representativeness of the findings, as the exclusion of patients with incomplete data might introduce bias. Another limitation is the lack of randomization, which increases the risk of selection bias. The study’s data-collection process was subject to human errors, though the large sample size is expected to mitigate their impact. The study’s focus on data from hospitals mostly within a single country with a disproportionate number of patients coming from Site 1 also decreases the generalizability of its findings to other healthcare systems or differing patient demographics. POD was measured using a screening tool in the PACU only and to fully assess the impact on POD, one would need to assess patients with clinically diagnosed events of POD up to 7 days post-surgery. Finally, we lacked information on rare but critical events such as aspiration, which are challenging to quantify and analyze due to their infrequency and the absence of comprehensive FFT data in large patient registries. CONCLUSION FFT can and should be improved in clinical practice as there are still too many patients with prolonged fasting times. Implementing short preoperative fasting times (2–4 hours) addresses patient concerns regarding discomfort and anxiety while potentially decreasing POD observed in the PACU. Additionally, short FFT may lead to cost savings by decreasing hospital stays. Consistently implementing this measure in clinical practice, with appropriate training for all involved parties, promotes patient-centered care delivery and may improve overall outcomes and satisfaction. documents.title: ESAIC pre-operative evaluation of adults undergoing elective non-cardiac surgery

chunks.content: Anaesthesiologists' guideline adherence in pre-operative evaluation: a retrospective observational study. Surveys suggest a low level of implementation of clinical guidelines, although they are intended to improve the quality of treatment and patient safety. Which guideline recommendations are not followed and why has yet to be analysed. In this study, we investigate the proportion of European and national guidelines followed in the area of pre-operative anaesthetic evaluation prior to non-cardiac surgery. We conducted this monocentric retrospective observational study at a German university hospital with the help of software that logically links guidelines in such a way that individualised recommendations can be derived from a patient's data. We included routine logs of 2003 patients who visited our pre-anaesthesia outpatient clinic between June 2018 and June 2020 and compared the actual conducted pre-operative examinations with the recommendations issued by the software. We descriptively analysed the data for examinations not performed that would have been recommended by the guidelines and examinations that were performed even though they were not covered by a guideline recommendation. The guidelines examined in this study are the 2018 ESAIC guidelines for pre-operative evaluation of adults undergoing elective non-cardiac surgery, the 2014 ESC/ESA guidelines on non-cardiac surgery and the German recommendations on pre-operative evaluation on non-cardiothoracic surgery from the year 2017. Performed ECG (78.1%) and cardiac stress imaging tests (86.1%) indicated the highest guideline adherence. Greater adherence rates were associated with a higher ASA score (ASA I: 23.7%, ASA II: 41.1%, ASA III: 51.8%, ASA IV: 65.8%, P < 0.001), lower BMI and age > 65 years. Adherence rates in high-risk surgery (60.5%) were greater than in intermediate (46.5%) or low-risk (44.6%) surgery (P < 0.001). 67.2% of technical and laboratory tests performed preoperatively were not covered by a guideline recommendation. Guideline adherence in pre-operative evaluation leaves room for improvement. Many performed pre-operative examinations, especially laboratory tests, are not recommended by the guidelines and may cause unnecessary costs. The reasons for guidelines not being followed may be the complexity of guidelines and organisational issues. A software-based decision support tool may be helpful. ClinicalTrials.gov ID NCT04843202.
